title: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
summary: LSASS Memory is the Windows specific credential dump that targets the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service process, where the system caches logon material after a user signs in. An adversary with administrative or SYSTEM rights opens the process, allocates memory inside it, and writes a dump file, or abuses a Windows mechanism such as the silent process exit feature to make the error reporting service produce the dump instead. Signed built-in utilities can perform the copy, so the process access itself is not automatically suspicious and the resulting file write is often the clearest artefact. Defenders correlate process access against the LSASS process, creation of dump files in unusual paths, registry changes that add a security support provider, and the parent process of whatever performed the access. Endpoint security products also read LSASS memory, so allow listing trusted tools by signature, path and behaviour is part of triage.

beginner.definition: LSASS is a Windows process that keeps login secrets in memory after you sign in. This sub-technique means copying that memory to steal the secrets. It is one specific way of stealing credentials, narrower than the parent because the source is a single running process.
beginner.whyItMatters: This one action can hand an attacker many working credentials at once. It usually needs administrator rights, so it marks a serious stage of an intrusion. Attackers often use built-in Windows tools, which can look legitimate. Ignoring it means the next step is often movement to other machines. Monitoring it well gives you an early warning of a much bigger attack.
howItWorks: A user signs in, and Windows stores login material inside the LSASS process memory.
The attacker gains administrator or SYSTEM rights on that computer.
They open the LSASS process and ask Windows to write its memory to a file.
Sometimes a built-in tool or a signed program is used to make the copy.
The dump file is taken away and read on another machine for passwords and hashes.
Registry settings for extra security packages may also be changed to capture logons.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel front desk with a notebook listing every guest key ever issued. A visitor with a staff pass photographs the whole notebook instead of stealing one key. The notebook stays on the desk and nothing looks missing. Back home, the visitor copies any key they need from the photographs. LSASS memory is that notebook: one copy gives the attacker many keys at once.
takeaways: LSASS memory holds many credentials, which makes it a high value target.
Look for unusual process access to LSASS and for new dump files on disk.
Signed tools can dump memory too, so check the caller, path and timing.

objectives: Explain what LSASS is and why it holds valuable credential material.
Describe how a memory dump is produced from a running process.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the OS credential dumping parent.
Identify process access and file creation events that reveal the technique.
Describe how to weigh legitimate security tooling against malicious access.
